questions.q: According to Salmond's definition, Jurisprudence is:
o: Only the practical application of statutes to specific cases
An abstract, general, and theoretical investigation seeking to lay bare the essential principles of law and the legal system
Only the study of criminal law
A purely historical record of past court judgments
questions.src: Salmond defined Jurisprudence as a theoretical, abstract investigation into law's essential principles, distinct from applying specific rules to specific cases.

questions.q: Salmond divided Jurisprudence into three branches. Which of the following is one of them?
o: Criminal, Civil, and Constitutional
Analytical, Historical, and Ethical
Federal, State, and Local
Domestic, International, and Comparative
questions.src: Salmond's three branches correspond to legal exposition (Analytical), history (Historical), and the science of legislation/what law ought to be (Ethical).

questions.q: The Analytical School of Jurisprudence, associated primarily with John Austin, is concerned with:
o: The historical origins of law only
Law "as it is" presently, without reference to its history or moral desirability
Only the moral content of law
Only customary practices of a community
questions.src: The Analytical/Positivist School focuses exclusively on existing (positum) law, deliberately setting aside historical origins and ethical evaluation.

questions.q: John Austin's Command Theory defines law as:
o: The general will of the people expressed through custom
The command of the sovereign, backed by sanction, issued to persons in a position of habitual obedience
Any rule a court happens to apply
A purely moral obligation with no state enforcement
questions.src: This is Austin's precise formulation — law as a sovereign command enforced through the threat of sanction.

questions.q: H.L.A. Hart refined legal positivism by distinguishing between:
o: Criminal law and civil law
Primary Rules (governing conduct) and Secondary Rules (rules about how primary rules are made/changed/adjudicated)
Written law and unwritten law only
Federal law and state law
questions.src: Hart's primary/secondary rules distinction addressed key gaps in Austin's simpler command-based theory.

questions.q: Savigny's "Volksgeist" theory, central to the Historical School, holds that law:
o: Should be artificially imposed by legislation regardless of custom
Grows organically from the common consciousness/spirit of a people, alongside their customs and character
Has no connection whatsoever to a community's history
Is entirely a product of judicial command
questions.src: Volksgeist ("spirit of the people") reflects Savigny's view that genuine law emerges organically from a community's lived experience, not top-down imposition.

questions.q: The maxim "Ubi societas ibi lex" ("where there is society, there is law") is associated with which school of jurisprudence?
o: Analytical School
Historical School
Realist School
None of these schools
questions.src: This maxim reflects the Historical School's view that law is an inevitable, organic byproduct of any organised community.

questions.q: Hugo Grotius, regarded as the father of the Philosophical/Natural Law School, argued that natural law springs from:
o: The arbitrary will of a sovereign ruler
The social nature of humanity itself, emerging from right reason
Purely economic considerations
Ancient customs alone, with no moral dimension
questions.src: Grotius grounded natural law in humanity's inherently social nature and rational capacity, distinct from positivist sovereign-command theories.

questions.q: Roscoe Pound's Theory of Social Engineering compares the role of lawyers/jurists to that of:
o: Soldiers enforcing strict rules
Engineers, who use expertise to structure society toward maximum satisfaction of human wants with minimum friction
Historians recording past events
Poets expressing abstract ideals
questions.src: Pound's central analogy treats law as a tool jurists actively use to engineer beneficial social outcomes, much as engineers structure physical works.

questions.q: Under Pound's theory, the THREE categories of interests requiring balance are:
o: Only Individual and Public interests
Individual, Public, and Social interests
Only religious and secular interests
Only economic and political interests
questions.src: Pound classified competing interests into Individual (of the person), Public (of the state), and Social (of society as a whole) categories.

questions.q: A "Jural Postulate" in Pound's theory refers to:
o: A binding statute passed by Parliament
A foundational assumption every civilised society's legal system rests upon (e.g., that others will not intentionally harm you)
A type of criminal punishment
A form of judicial precedent
questions.src: Jural postulates are the basic, taken-for-granted assumptions (like freedom from intentional aggression) underlying a functioning legal system.

questions.q: "Legal Sources" of law, as distinguished from "Historical Sources," refer to sources:
o: That influenced law's development but are not themselves directly binding today
RECOGNISED by law itself as currently authoritative and binding (legislation, precedent, recognised custom)
Only ancient religious texts
Only foreign legal systems
questions.src: Legal sources carry present binding authority, while historical sources merely influenced law's development without being directly binding now.

questions.q: "Subordinate Legislation" refers to law made by:
o: The supreme/sovereign legislative body itself, with no higher authority
A body/authority exercising powers DELEGATED by the supreme legislature, remaining subject to its control
Only foreign governments
Judges deciding individual cases
questions.src: Subordinate legislation is made under delegated authority and remains subject to the supreme legislature's ultimate oversight/control.

questions.q: An "Original Precedent," as distinguished from a "Declaratory Precedent," is one that:
o: Merely restates an already-established legal principle
Establishes a genuinely NEW legal principle for the first time
Has no binding force whatsoever
Can only come from a foreign court
questions.src: Original precedents break new ground by establishing a principle not previously recognised, unlike declaratory precedents which apply existing principles.

questions.q: An "Authoritative Precedent," as distinguished from a "Persuasive Precedent," is one that:
o: Judges may freely ignore at their own discretion
Judges are BOUND to follow, per the doctrine of binding precedent within the same court hierarchy
Has no legal significance
Only applies to criminal cases
questions.src: Authoritative precedents carry binding force on courts within the relevant hierarchy, unlike merely persuasive precedents from other jurisdictions/courts.

questions.q: For a custom to be recognised as a valid legal source, it must generally satisfy requirements including:
o: Only that it be popular, with no other conditions
Antiquity, continuity, reasonableness, certainty, and consistency with statute law
Only that a single person has followed it
That it contradicts existing statute law
questions.src: These five requirements collectively ensure a custom is genuinely long-standing, consistently observed, fair, definite, and compatible with enacted law before courts will recognise it as legally binding.

questions.q: A legal RIGHT "in rem," as distinguished from a right "in personam," is available:
o: Only against one specific, determinate person
Against the world at large (e.g., ownership of property, enforceable against anyone who interferes)
Only in criminal proceedings
Only to government entities
questions.src: Rights in rem bind everyone generally, while rights in personam bind only specific determinate persons, such as the other party to a contract.

questions.q: Under Hohfeld's analysis of legal relations, a "Right" correlates directly with a:
o: Privilege
Duty (if A has a right, B has a corresponding duty)
Power
Immunity
questions.src: Hohfeld's framework pairs Right with Duty as direct correlatives, along with three other correlative pairs (Privilege-NoRight, Power-Liability, Immunity-Disability).

questions.q: A "Legal/Juristic Person," as distinguished from a "Natural Person," refers to:
o: Only human beings
An entity OTHER than a human being that law treats as capable of holding rights/duties (e.g., a corporation)
Only government officials
A person who has died
questions.src: Juristic persons are non-human entities (corporations, societies, and in some legal traditions even certain deities) recognised by law as capable of holding legal rights and duties.

questions.q: The two essential elements of legal "Possession" are generally identified as:
o: Ownership and title
Corpus Possessionis (physical control) and Animus Possidendi (intention to hold/exclude others)
Registration and taxation
Inheritance and gift
questions.src: Both physical control (corpus) and the mental intention to possess/exclude others (animus) are generally required for legal possession to exist.

questions.q: "Possession," as distinguished from "Ownership," is best described as a matter of:
o: Right, exactly the same as ownership
FACT (actual physical control with requisite intent), while ownership is a matter of RIGHT (the fullest legal title)
Pure religious doctrine
Government permission only
questions.src: This is the fundamental distinction — possession concerns factual control, while ownership concerns the legally recognised entitlement/title itself.

questions.q: A thief who has stolen goods generally has:
o: Both ownership AND possession of the goods
Possession of the goods, but NOT ownership
Ownership of the goods, but not possession
Neither possession nor ownership
questions.src: This illustrates the divergence between possession (fact) and ownership (right) — a thief can factually possess goods without ever acquiring legal ownership of them.

questions.q: "Mediate (Indirect) Possession" refers to possession exercised:
o: Personally, without any intermediary
THROUGH another person (e.g., an owner's possession exercised through a bailee holding goods on their behalf)
Only over intangible rights
Only by government bodies
questions.src: Mediate possession involves an intermediary (like a bailee) holding the thing on behalf of the person actually exercising possession through them.

questions.q: "Civil Liability," as distinguished from "Criminal Liability," generally results in:
o: Imprisonment imposed by the state
An obligation to pay compensation/damages to the injured party (remedial)
The death penalty
No consequence whatsoever
questions.src: Civil liability is fundamentally remedial/compensatory, aiming to restore the injured party, distinct from criminal liability's punitive, state-imposed consequences.

questions.q: "Absolute Ownership," as distinguished from "Limited Ownership," refers to ownership that is:
o: Restricted by a specific time-limit or condition
Unrestricted by any time-limit or condition
Only available to corporations
Only recognised in criminal law
questions.src: Absolute ownership carries no built-in temporal or conditional restriction, unlike limited ownership (e.g., a life interest lasting only for someone's lifetime).

questions.q: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) is jurisprudentially significant because it directly tested:
o: The doctrine of custom as a source of law
Austin's Command Theory's assumption of an unlimited sovereign, against a constitutional order where even Parliament's amending power is bounded by a 'basic structure'
The distinction between civil and criminal liability
The concept of possession versus ownership
questions.src: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (Supreme Court, 1973) — held Parliament's amending power, however broad, is not an unlimited Austinian sovereign power, illustrating the tension between Command Theory and a constitutional Rule of Law

questions.q: In Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee v. Som Nath Dass (2000), the Supreme Court held that the Guru Granth Sahib:
o: Cannot be recognised as a juristic person under any circumstances
Could be recognised as a juristic person, illustrating that legal personality extends to entities other than human beings when genuinely recognised by their community
Is identical in legal status to a natural person
Has no bearing on Indian jurisprudence regarding legal persons
questions.src: Shiromani Gurdwara Prabandhak Committee v. Som Nath Dass (Supreme Court, 2000) — extended juristic personality to the Guru Granth Sahib, applying the abstract Natural Person/Juristic Person distinction to real facts
